 Extended school holiday testing parenting, ‘supervising’ children 
 By 
 James Kandoya
 ,
 The Guardian 
 Published at 03:21 PM Nov 18 2026 
 File 
 students 
 THE extended school holiday following the early closure of schools across the country has placed fresh responsibilities on parents to keep children occupied, safe and engaged, while raising questions about the effects of spending nearly two months away from structured classroom learning.
 With pre-primary, primary and secondary schools closing on November 13, instead of the previously scheduled December 4, pupils now have a longer period at home, presenting both an opportunity for personal development and a challenge for families, particularly those whose parents have demanding work schedules.
 While the break offers children time to rest after a lengthy academic year, education and parenting stakeholders say prolonged periods without structured activities can expose them to harmful influences, weaken study routines and increase the burden on parents to provide guidance and supervision.
 Evelyne Shomari, a mother of two, said she planned to enrol her children in alternative education programmes and short courses, including life skills training, to ensure they continued learning outside the classroom.
 She said the extended break provided an opportunity for children to acquire practical knowledge and competencies that might not be adequately covered through formal classroom instruction.
 Another parent, Mariam Salehe, said she intended to involve her children in household chores and small business activities to develop responsibility, discipline and self-reliance.
 She said keeping children engaged in meaningful family activities would help them appreciate the value of work and prepare them for future responsibilities rather than spending most of their time on entertainment.
 Parenting expert and Ruffon Social Worker Director Hilda Ngaja said the extended holiday required parents to become more deliberate about their children's upbringing, particularly by providing guidance and setting positive examples.
 She noted that children often imitate the behaviour of adults around them, making parental involvement essential in shaping their attitudes, values and decision-making.
  Ngaja also cautioned that spending more time away from school could expose children to negative peer influence, inappropriate online content and violence if parents failed to monitor their activities.
 She urged parents to pay closer attention to their children's friendships, social media use and television consumption, while creating opportunities for open communication and positive interaction.
 She said supervision should not simply involve restricting children's movements but also teaching them responsible behaviour and helping them distinguish between acceptable and harmful influences.
 Meanwhile, Greyson Mgoy of Uwezo Tanzania said school holidays were primarily intended to give pupils time to rest and recover after lengthy academic terms.
 However, he advised parents to maintain flexible learning routines to prevent children from completely losing touch with their studies.
 He encouraged families to set aside time for reading, reviewing exercise books and textbooks, while allowing children sufficient opportunities for recreation and other activities.
 Other contributors suggested that parents consider enrolling their children in short vocational programmes, including courses offered by the Vocational Education and Training Authority (VETA), to equip them with practical and technical skills.
 They said a combination of academic revision, recreation, vocational training and household responsibilities could help children use the extended break constructively.
 Despite the government-directed closure date, some schools have reportedly opted to extend learning activities until December 27, raising questions about how institutions and parents are responding to the unusually long break.
 The decision by such schools to continue learning activities reflects differing approaches to managing the interruption of the academic calendar, although it also raises the need for clarity on compliance with official education directives.
 The early closure was communicated through an education circular issued by Commissioner for Education Dr Lyabwene Mtahabwa, directing schools to close on November 13 for the term ending in December 2026, bringing forward the original December 4 date.
 The decision was aimed at safeguarding the safety and welfare of pupils, teachers and other school employees.
 The development means families must now shoulder a greater share of responsibility for children's daily routines, particularly in households where both parents work or where access to organised holiday programmes is limited.
 For parents, the challenge is therefore not simply keeping children busy but ensuring that the extended break does not become a period of excessive screen time, idleness or exposure to unsafe environments.
 The holiday also presents an opportunity for families to strengthen relationships with children through shared activities, conversations, reading, household responsibilities and the development of practical life skills.
 As pupils spend more time outside the classroom, the effectiveness of parental guidance and community support will be important in determining whether the extended break becomes an opportunity for growth or a period of lost learning and increased exposure to risks.
